name: scenario.acid.isolation_read_phenomena

name: scenario.acid.row_locks

FOR UPDATE / UPDATE / DELETE: FOR UPDATE NOWAIT, NO_WAIT and WAIT 1 fail with 1205 'Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction'; FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED returns (and locks) the other rows; non-locking reads never block and see the committed row; ob_trx_lock_timeout (microseconds) bounds UPDATE / DELETE / INSERT / FOR UPDATE waits with 1205, rolling back only that statement; new keys and other rows are not blocked; LOCK IN SHARE MODE conflicts with FOR UPDATE, UPDATE and another LOCK IN SHARE MODE; locks are released at COMMIT and ROLLBACK; innodb_lock_wait_timeout is a mock (SET gives warning 1235, value stays 50) | suspected original bug (recorded as is): LOCK IN SHARE MODE takes an exclusive row lock: after c1 'select * from rl_t where id = 2 lock in share mode', c2 'select * from rl_t where id = 2 lock in share mode' (ob_trx_lock_timeout = 1000000) fails with 1205 (MySQL lets two share-mode readers coexist); 'set session innodb_lock_wait_timeout = 1' only returns Warning 1235 'This system variable now is mock not supported' and the value stays 50, so the MySQL way of bounding lock waits has no effect | Gray area: uses the public ob_ system variable ob_trx_lock_timeout (listed in ob_system_variable_init.json) as the public equivalent of innodb_lock_wait_timeout. name: scenario.acid.write_conflicts

FOR UPDATE returns the latest committed row; first-updater-wins under REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: UPDATE or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE of a row changed after the snapshot fails with 6235 'can't serialize access for this transaction', only the statement is rolled back and the transaction commits its other writes; if the first updater rolls back the waiter succeeds; rows inserted after a REPEATABLE READ snapshot are not returned by FOR UPDATE nor touched by UPDATE without WHERE (affected rows 3), a row deleted after the snapshot makes both fail with 6235; write skew succeeds under SERIALIZABLE and REPEATABLE READ; a concurrent INSERT of the same key waits, then 1062 if the first inserter commits or success if it rolls back | suspected original bug (recorded as is): SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation and allows write skew: two SERIALIZABLE transactions both read 'select sum(on_call) from wc_oncall' = 2, one runs 'update wc_oncall set on_call = 0 where doctor = 'alice'', the other '... where doctor = 'bob'', both COMMIT succeed and the sum becomes 0 (ANSI / MySQL SERIALIZABLE would block or fail one of them); probably by design (Oracle-style) but it deviates from MySQL | Blocking statements are sent with send, given --exec sleep 1 to reach their lock wait, then reaped after the other session ends; every expected value is the same whether or not the statement had started waiting.
